articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Jairam Ramesh on Thursday questioned what he described as conflicting statements by senior military officials on the extent of cooperation between Pakistan and China during Operation Sindoor.Sharing video clips on X, Ramesh said Deputy Chief of Army Staff Lt Gen Rahul Singh had, on July 4, 2025, highlighted what he called the “very disturbingly deep nature” of the Pakistan-China partnership during the military operation.The Congress leader contrasted those remarks with comments made by former Chief of Defence Staff Gen. Anil Chauhan on August 25, 2026, saying Chauhan's account appeared to be “simply opposite” to that of Lt. Gen. Singh.“On July 4 2025, the Deputy Chief of Army Staff Lt. Gen Rahul Singh had revealed the very disturbingly deep nature of the Pakistan-China jugalbandi during Operation Sindoor. On Aug 25, 2026, the former Chief of Defence Staff Gen. Anil Chauhan made his own revelations on this jugalbandi - which are simply opposite to what Lt. Gen Singh had said. The nation is confused," said Ramesh on X.The Congress leader questioned whether the differing accounts reflected a broader effort to shape the public narrative around India's relations with China.“What is going on here? Is there some deeper plan to change the narrative?” he asked.He also linked the issue to the Centre's broader China policy, alleging that there had been a “calibrated capitulation to China” and citing what he described as the Prime Minister's “infamous clean chit to China on June 2020” as well as India's record trade deficits with China.Ramesh's remarks came ex-CDS Chauhan, speaking at the ‘VIMARSH’ event on Operation Sindoor and its aftermath at the Vivekananda International Foundation, said Pakistan had failed to obtain evidence of the targets struck by India despite attempts to access commercial satellite imagery.Chauhan said the presence of Chinese personnel supporting Pakistan's military equipment during Operation Sindoor should be viewed in the context of "contractual obligations", while cautioning against drawing conclusions beyond established facts.In the clip shared by Ramesh, General Singh can be heard stating that the key lessons from Operation Sindoor were that India faced a multi-adversary challenge, with Pakistan at the forefront and China and Turkey providing significant military support. He added that China also used the conflict to assess its weapons and systems in a real-world environment.India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, 2025, days after the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack that killed 26 people. The operation targeted terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK).Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A Michigan businessman brought nine white-tailed deer to North Manitou Island in 1926; decades later, the artificial herd had grown to an estimated 2,000
articles.summary: US News: North Manitou Island was never home to large game until a wealthy Michigan businessman decided it should be. In the mid-1920s, William R. Angell, the .
articles.body: North Manitou Island was never home to large game until a wealthy Michigan businessman decided it should be. In the mid-1920s, William R. Angell, the driving force behind the Manitou Island Association, set out to turn the 15,000-acre island into a private hunting and fishing retreat for himself and his associates. His answer was to bring white-tailed deer to a landscape that had never supported them, nine animals shipped over from the mainland with no natural predators waiting on the other side. What began as a modest experiment in stocking a sportsman's playground would, within a few decades, grow into one of the largest deer herds ever recorded on an island of its size, reaching an estimated 2,000 by the early 1980s and forcing a reckoning between private ambition and the land's own limits. That story starts with Angell himself, and the choices he made in 1926.How William R. Angell brought nine white-tailed deer to North Manitou IslandIn the mid-1920s, businessman William R. Angell set in motion one of the most consequential wildlife experiments in the history of North Manitou Island. Angell, the principal owner behind the Manitou Island Association, wanted to turn the 15,000-acre island into an exclusive retreat where he and his associates could hunt and fish away from the mainland crowds. White-tailed deer were central to that ambition, and in 1926 he had a small founding herd brought over to establish the population from scratch.As per The Leelanau Historical Society, a slightly fuller account of the same event, recording that the white-tailed fawns were sourced from the Munising State Forest and arrived nine strong, eight does and a single buck, chosen in the hope that their bloodline would eventually produce impressive racks for hunters to pursue. Whichever figure is taken as the precise starting point, both accounts agree that the white-tailed deer were an entirely artificial addition to an island that had never supported large game before.How deer became the main attraction for wealthy sportsmenAngell's motive for introducing deer was never purely sentimental. He and his fellow landowners in the Manitou Island Association were building a business, and a stocked hunting ground was the product they wished to sell. Raccoons had already been released in 1924 for the same purpose, but it was the deer that would come to define the island's reputation among wealthy sportsmen throughout the following decades.The early years were not without difficulty. Farm dogs on the island reportedly killed three of the original fawns when they tried to herd the newcomers as though they were cattle, mistaking their unfamiliar behaviour for something that needed correcting. Once that initial disruption passed, however, the surviving deer found ideal conditions on North Manitou. With no natural predators and abundant vegetation to browse, the small founding group began to multiply at a pace that would soon outstrip the island's capacity to support them.How nine deer grew to 700 on North Manitou IslandUnchecked breeding transformed Angell's modest founding stock into a genuine management problem within little more than a decade. By 1937, the population had swollen to an estimated 700 animals, prompting the Manitou Island Association to organise the island's first official deer hunt with assistance from the State of Michigan, alongside a winter supplemental feeding programme to keep the herd alive through the harsher months. By the 1950s that figure had climbed to around 1,000, and naturalists and state officials returned periodically over the following decades to count the herd and assess its condition.The growth did not stop there. According to the National Park Service, "By counts in the early 1980s, there were about 2,000 deer on the island," a scale that had visibly reshaped the landscape itself. The deer stripped the island of almost every plant they found palatable, leaving a distinctive browse line five to six feet above the ground and allowing unpalatable species such as American beech to flourish unchecked in their place, a stark contrast to the lush understorey still found on neighbouring South Manitou Island.Why North Manitou Island became a private hunting retreatFor much of the twentieth century, the herd Angell had founded served a narrow and well-heeled clientele. Hunters were generally guests of the island's principal owners or corporate clients drawn from firms such as Continental Motors and Shakespeare Rod and Reel, along with government contractors and, during the 1950s and 1960s, associates of the Detroit mafia. Each guest was guaranteed a deer, driven out to a guide-selected spot in the morning and returned to the lodge for lunch before an evening of cards and conversation. Guides ensured a steady supply for the table by shooting animals from moving vehicles when demand outpaced what visiting hunters managed to bag themselves.That arrangement could not survive the island's transfer into public ownership. Negotiations between the Manitou Island Association and the US Justice Department over incorporating the island into the Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore began in 1977 and dragged on for seven contentious years, and when the Association withdrew its staff in the autumn of 1978, the supplemental feeding programme that had sustained Angell's herd through the winters came to an abrupt end. Hundreds of deer and turkeys starved over the two winters that followed, a grim coda to a herd that had begun, half a century earlier, as a handful of fawns brought ashore for the pleasure of a wealthy few.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump administration pauses all immigrant visa applications amid new screening policy
articles.summary: The pause began in early August and is not expected to last beyond early to mid-September, according to a State Department official not authorized to speak publicly about the change.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration has trained much of its immigration crackdown on people who entered the United States illegally from Mexico and elsewhere, but it is intensifying another battle, this time with people who come legally. The State Department has paused all immigrant visa applications while it briefs consular officials around the world on a new policy that aims to keep out people who are considered potential drains on public coffers. The administration is also preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who applied for asylum, which The Associated Press first reported this week. It would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history and would likely face legal challenges. “The thing linking them is a general philosophy that immigration is bad for the United States and that the Trump administration is looking for all of the ways it can to button down our immigration system to allow in fewer people,” said Julia Gelatt, associate director of the U.S. immigration policy program at the Migration Policy Institute. The pause in issuing immigrant visas is expected to be temporary The pause is related entirely to new rules about a “public charge” requirement that numerous consular officers in U.S. embassies around the world had questions about, according to a State Department official who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. It began in early August and is not expected to last beyond early to mid-September, the official said, noting that most people affected by the pause had interviews scheduled for August but that none of them had been canceled. Those interviews will be rescheduled for September, October and November. Anybody applying for an immigrant visa outside the U.S. could be affected by the pause, experts said, mainly those seeking to come on family grounds, including parents, spouses, children or siblings of U.S. citizens. Gelatt cautioned, though, that rescheduling a visa appointment may not be easy. “They’re hard to get, and so having to reschedule is a big challenge for people,” she said. Other types of immigrant visas, like those for workers who have an employer sponsoring them, are not affected because they can demonstrate earnings and would not be a “public charge.” “We need to see how long this pause lasts. It sounded like it would be short, just to make time for training, but if it does last longer, I imagine we’ll see litigation,” Gelatt said. A policy that halted the issuance of visas to immigrants from 75 countries was in place from January to mid-August, when a court struck it down. It could be seen as a precedent. In tightening the public charge rules, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security, revived a rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits such as food stamps, Medicaid and housing vouchers. Revoking tourism and business visas will ‘send a message’ Unless the decision is challenged or revised, the State Department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by The Associated Press and two U.S. officials. The action will be taken in coordination with DHS. The State Department has not said how many visas will be revoked, but some experts and immigration lawyers point out that the measure will have no consequences for those already in the United States who have applied for asylum. “The goal is instead to send a message that this administration is focused on enforcement and that people who want to live in the United States should not think about coming on a tourist visa and then seeking asylum,” Gelatt said. “For people who already have a tourist visa that’s being revoked, it really is not going to affect them because they already have lodged their asylum application and are waiting in line for that asylum adjudication. The temporary visa really doesn’t matter anymore.” Asylum claims can take years to decide. Tourist and business visas, on the other hand, allowed stays of about six months. If the visa holders request asylum, their ability to stay in the U.S. depends on their open asylum cases and not on their visas, according to experts. For years, people who apply for tourist or business visas have had to demonstrate to U.S. officials that they plan to return home when their time expires. Any indication that they wish to stay permanently is grounds for denying their visa. Plans to revoke visas are consistent with Trump’s long-held belief that asylum is largely a sham. “People in the U.S. and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims. Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration laws,” Christopher Landau, a deputy secretary of state, said Monday. In April, the administration said consulates would deny visas to applicants who indicate they were afraid to go home.

articles.title: PM Modi to meet Putin on SCO summit sidelines during Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan visit
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic from August 29 to September 1, the ministry of external affairs .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic from August 29 to September 1, the ministry of external affairs said on Thursday.During his four-day visit, PM Modi will undertake a bilateral visit to Tashkent and participate in the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek.PM Modi will also hold bilateral meetings with SCO leaders on the sidelines of the summit. According to news agency PTI, Putin will also be among the leaders with whom PM Modi will hold bilateral meetings on the margins of the summit.PM Modi is also expected to visit the Shastri Memorial in Tashkent and the Mahatma Gandhi Centre at the Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies.This will be PM Modi's fourth visit and his second bilateral visit to Uzbekistan, according to MEA Secretary (West) Sibi George.Addressing a special briefing on the Prime Minister's visit, MEA Secretary (West) said India and Uzbekistan have maintained "extensive and fruitful engagements" over the years in both bilateral and multilateral formats.Highlighting the depth of economic ties, the MEA Secretary said India is among Uzbekistan's top 10 trading partners, with bilateral trade and investments together close to USD 1 billion."We have wide-ranging cooperation in the fields of critical minerals, pharma, education, information technology, and the health sector," he said.The summit coincides with the SCO's 25th anniversary of its founding. After serving as an observer since 2005, India became a full member of the organisation in 2017.From August 31 to September 1, the Prime Minister will visit Bishkek, George stated.According to the MEA, the organisation's main goal was to combat the three "evils" of terrorism, separatism and extremism, which continue to present challenges.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Jynxzi spent years streaming Rainbow Six Siege to tiny audiences; then, TikTok clips turned him into Twitch's most subscribed creator
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Jynxzi, whose real name is Nicholas Stewart, did not become one of Twitch’s biggest names by jumping from trend to trend. His rise came from sticking .
articles.body: Jynxzi, whose real name is Nicholas Stewart, did not become one of Twitch’s biggest names by jumping from trend to trend. His rise came from sticking with Rainbow Six Siege and finding a smarter way to get people into his livestreams. For years, the grind looked almost invisible. Then short-form clips changed the game, giving his streams a steady path to much bigger audiences. By April 2023, that strategy had taken him past names like Kai Cenat, xQc, and HasanAbi, putting him at No. 1 among Twitch creators by subscriptions. He also crossed 150,000 active paid subscribers and regularly reached more than 80,000 viewers at the same time. The interesting part is that none of this started with huge live numbers.The early years were basically Jynxzi talking to a tiny roomStewart started streaming full-time on Twitch in January 2019. He focused completely on Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Siege, even though the numbers were rough. For roughly three years, he could stream for 10 to 12 hours a day and still average only around 10 to 50 viewers.That was the part most people never saw. Instead of dropping Siege for whatever game was hot, Stewart stayed with it. He kept working on the same title and learned how to make its technical, tactical gameplay entertaining. The audience was small, but the commitment did not change. That loyalty eventually became the base for everything that followed.Then he stopped waiting for Twitch to discover himLate in 2022, Stewart changed how he looked at growth. Rather than expecting Twitch itself to send new viewers his way, he began using TikTok and YouTube Shorts as a funnel for his livestreams.The idea was pretty simple. Take the loudest, funniest, most chaotic moments from a stream and turn them into clips people would actually stop for.His team posted as many as three to five edited clips every day. The content also pushed a very clear personality. Aggressive chair slaps, intense facecam shots and memorable catchphrases made the videos easy to recognize.That short-form system gave people a reason to discover Jynxzi before they ever opened his Twitch stream.The numbers changed fast once the clips started feeding the live channelThe payoff was massive. By April 2023, Jynxzi had moved ahead of Kai Cenat, xQc and HasanAbi to become Twitch’s most-subscribed creator.His peak numbers were even wilder. He passed 150,000 paying subscribers and regularly pulled more than 80,000 concurrent viewers. Rainbow Six Siege also benefited from the attention, seeing a major revival in players and viewership. His broadcasts eventually led to collaborations with Ubisoft.The stream itself was no longer the only product. The clips had become the front door.Jynxzi kept building after the Twitch breakthroughHe later expanded the brand with The 20Vs1 Podcast, where internet personalities appeared on a dating and interview-style show that pulled millions of views per episode.He also created wager matches and tournaments around the Siege community, bringing pro players and mainstream influencers together.Then came the business move. Jynxzi joined Spacestation Gaming as a co-owner and content creator, taking his career further into esports.His story is a long grind that only became visible after the short-form machine finally started pointing millions of eyes toward it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Social enterprise revives vacant Galashiels building
articles.summary: The ceiling of the property in Galashiels had collapsed before the Hike & Bike Hub moved in.
articles.body:
A cycling social enterprise is bringing one of the biggest eyesore buildings in the Scottish Borders back into use.

The community led Hike & Bike Hub purchased the site at Douglas Bridge in Galashiels with the help of South of Scotland Enterprise (SOSE) at the start of the year.

The ceiling in the building had collapsed and it had been a regular target for vandalism.

Co-founder Angela Crow said she was happy to play her part in helping to regenerate the town centre.

The move to a larger base will allow the organisation to expand its bike hire, maintenance and training services, while also offering more guided cycle rides and walking experiences.

During his visit, Business Minister Tom Arthur praised the organisation's impact on the community.

"With support from SOSE, Hike & Bike's new base in Galashiels offers renewed opportunities not just to support the Borders' thriving biking scene and associated tourism, but to be a focal point and trusted partner for people and businesses across the town and wider region," he said.

The project received support from SOSE, including assistance with its business plan and a £140,000 grant.

The purchase has brought a prominent empty building back into use and contributed to wider regeneration work in the town.

Russel Griggs, who chairs SOSE, said: "The Hike & Bike Hub is a great example of the kind of ambitious, community-led enterprise that is making a real difference across the south of Scotland.

"The organisation is bringing so much to Galashiels, supporting active lifestyles, helping neurodiverse young people, aiding community regeneration and contributing to the local visitor economy."

Future plans include the creation of four bunkhouse-style rooms, including one fully accessible ground-floor room.

Crow said: "This is a hugely exciting time for us, with our plans to redevelop the building, and offer new visitor accommodation in Galashiels, contributing to our longer-term viability."

The social enterprise's work has also earned recognition, with Hike & Bike Hub shortlisted for a South of Scotland Thistle Award in the Best Community Tourism and Events Experience category.

articles.summary: Bryan Kohberger faces key deadlines as Idaho judge outlines how his attempt to withdraw his guilty plea will proceed, with a hearing tentatively set.
articles.body: In an order outlining how Bryan Kohberger's attempt to withdraw his guilty plea will play out in court, Idaho Judge Steven Hippler revealed that the hearings scheduled this week for June 2027 are not set in stone as he set a number of deadlines in coming months and told the sides what he expects of them. "If an evidentiary hearing is granted, it shall be set to commence on June 17, 2027, at 9:00 a.m.," he wrote. Prosecutors have asked him not to grant a hearing, describing Kohberger's claims as "bare, conclusory and unsupported by admissible evidence." Kohberger, 31, last year pleaded guilty to four counts of first-degree murder and a felony burglary charge for the 2022 stabbing deaths of University of Idaho students Madison Mogen, 21, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20. BRYAN KOHBERGER GETS NEW ATTORNEY APPOINTED AFTER HE ASKS COURT FOR POST-CONVICTION RELIEF IN IDAHO MURDERS In a motion filed Tuesday, Deputy Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl asked for a transcript of Kohberger's July 2, 2025, change of plea hearing, in which Kohberger's own words could be used to rebut the new claims in his petition. Kohberger, in a handwritten petition filed in July, is claiming he had ineffective counsel, that his guilty plea was "not knowingly or voluntarily entered because it was induced by unkept promises" and that it was "not voluntarily entered because of threats asserted by petitioner's (Kohberger's) legal counsel." BRYAN KOHBERGER'S POST-CONVICTION RELIEF BID ENABLED BY FLAWED PLEA DEAL, PSYCHOLOGIST ARGUES But in 2025, Kohberger checked "no" when asked whether an attorney or anyone else had forced or coerced him into accepting the plea agreement or made other promises that influenced his decision. He affirmed that there was nothing going on in his life that would impair his ability to enter his guilty plea voluntarily, and there was no reason he couldn't make a "reasoned and informed decision" when he did so. Read the state's motion to dismiss Kohberger's petition for post conviction relief: Scholl asked Hippler to dismiss Kohberger's petition outright. "The petition fails to raise a genuine issue of material fact, and respondent is entitled to judgment as a matter of law," he wrote. He said Kohberger's petition included no facts to support his claim that he had ineffective counsel and wrote that Kohberger's "freestanding claim of actual innocence" is unrecognized under the law. articles.title: Texas police officer indicted on 100 felony counts after Flock investigation; records show over 45,000 searches, including nearly 3,500 for one licence plate
articles.summary: US News: A Lufkin, Texas police officer has been indicted on 100 felony counts after an investigation into his use of Flock Safety’s automated license plate re.
articles.body: A Lufkin, Texas police officer has been indicted on 100 felony counts after an investigation into his use of Flock Safety’s automated license plate reader system revealed an extraordinary volume of searches, including nearly 3,500 lookups of a single licence plate. According to court records and audit logs reviewed by the Houston Chronicle and local Texas outlets, 32-year-old Officer Zachary Anthony Klein conducted more than 45,000 searches over roughly 200 days, far exceeding typical usage patterns in the department. He was charged last week with misuse of official information, prompting the Lufkin Police Department to suspend its use of Flock entirely and call in the Texas Rangers for an independent review. The case has reignited debates over surveillance, privacy and accountability as similar allegations surface in other Texas cities.An unusually high volume of searchesAccording to a Chron review of audit logs published on the Have I Been Flocked platform, Klein conducted approximately 45,318 license plate reader searches between May 2024 and December 2025. That averages to about 1,258 searches per week, or roughly 74 searches per day, over the period reviewed.His profile shows he conducted more searches than any other officer in the Lufkin Police Department. By comparison, one of the Houston Police Department’s most frequent Flock users conducted only 361 searches a week, according to the same data.The database also reveals that Klein looked up the same four licence plates thousands of times, with one plate searched a total of 3,470 times in the course of a year. Flock requires officers to provide a reason for each search, such as kidnapping, robbery or auto theft. However, on Klein’s profile, the only reason he listed was “investigation.”Indictment and arrestAn Angelina County grand jury indicted Klein last week on 100 felony counts of misuse of official information related to the Flock license plate reader system, according to local reporting. He was arrested and booked into the Angelina County Jail on August 20, with bail set at $700,000.It remains unclear whether the highlighted licence plates belonged to people Klein knew personally, as the Chron has not confirmed the identities behind the most-searched plates. The department has not released detailed specifics about the targets of the searches beyond what appears in the public audit logs.Department suspends Flock, calls in Texas RangersIn response to the findings, Lufkin Police Chief Travis Brazil said the department has suspended its use of Flock entirely while internal affairs officers conduct an investigation. A second Lufkin officer has been placed on administrative leave following the investigation, according to the chief’s statement.Chief Brazil has also called on the Texas Rangers to perform a separate, independent investigation into the matter. The City of Lufkin originally approved the Flock camera system for departmental use in 2023, intending the AI-assisted surveillance technology to capture licence plates and vehicle details that may help generate leads into criminal investigations.Part of a broader pattern in TexasLufkin is now about the seventh Texas law enforcement agency in recent months to investigate allegations of officer misconduct related to Flock, according to the Chron. Several cases have involved allegations that officers used the network to stalk people in their personal lives, underscoring the growing privacy concerns citizens frequently associate with Flock.The rapid deployment of Flock cameras in neighborhoods, public roads and shopping centers has prompted cases where officers can use the network to track people and build a profile of their location history. Civil rights advocates say that level of surveillance typically requires a warrant, and in bad-faith scenarios, officers are accused of using it to stalk romantic partners or close associates, as per reports.Flock responds with new accountability featuresFlock Safety CEO Garrett Langley has addressed the issue in a recent interview with The Washington Post, acknowledging the risks that come with giving law enforcement powerful search tools.“It gets to this issue that when you are given power, which many people are, particularly in law enforcement, you should have higher standards of accountability,” Langley said, as per reports. “And so, I don’t think Flock created police abuse. I think we’re the first company to ever shine a light on it and build the tools to find it.”Langley said Flock is rolling out new features intended to increase accountability, including an internal audit system designed to flag unusual officer searches. The company has also reduced its standard data-retention period from 30 days to seven days, with some exceptions for ongoing investigations. Flock’s national law enforcement search system now also requires users to enter a case code before conducting a search.What happens next in LufkinFor now, the criminal case against Klein will proceed through the Angelina County courts, while the Texas Rangers conduct their independent review. The internal affairs investigation within the Lufkin Police Department is ongoing, and the department has not indicated whether additional disciplinary actions beyond the suspension of Flock and the administrative leave of a second officer are planned.The case is likely to intensify local debate over the use of automated licence plate readers and the safeguards needed to prevent misuse. As more audit logs become publicly accessible through platforms like Have I Been Flocked, communities and oversight bodies may push for stricter policies, more frequent audits and clearer consequences for officers who abuse access to surveillance databases.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ICE officer charged in Minneapolis shooting released in Texas after immediate extradition rejected
articles.summary: A day earlier, a judge wrote in an order that said he couldn’t prevent a county sheriff from releasing Christian Castro or order Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to sign his extradition warrant.
articles.body: BROWNSVILLE, Texas — An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with shooting a man and lying about it during the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis was released from a Texas jail Thursday, after a judge refused to order his return to Minnesota. Christian Castro was released at the break of dawn from a detention center in Brownsville. He motioned his hand toward a few camera operators and a reporter crowding around him and quickly got into an SUV that drove off. A day earlier, U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. wrote in an order that said he couldn’t prevent a county sheriff from releasing Castro or order Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to sign his extradition warrant. Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis. Castro is accused of firing a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg. Prosecutors say Castro also falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel. After a Minnesota judge issued a nationwide warrant for Castro’s arrest in May, authorities, including Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, arrested Castro in Cameron County on May 29. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since his arrest, but he remained in custody in Brownsville, a city bordering Mexico. Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro had to be released after 90 days of detention, which was Thursday. Minnesota officials believe Castro could flee to Mexico. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week seeking to block Castro’s release or to order his return to Minnesota. Texas attorneys on Tuesday argued the judge could not rule on a decision that’s still pending. Abbott has not denied the extradition. Instead he is waiting for the outcome of an internal state investigation considering whether Castro was legally a “fugitive” under the Extradition Clause, the lawyers said. The judge wrote in Wednesday’s order that the court couldn’t yet step in. “The Court concludes that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction because the case is not ripe for adjudication,” the order read. “Minnesota cannot premise its causes of action on the allegation that Governor Abbott may violate those authorities in the future; it must prove that a violation has already occurred.” The judge said in his order that the extradition laws do not outline how long the Texas governor can take to make that decision. Abbott said last week he would not respond to the extradition request, citing the ongoing investigation into fraud in government social service programs in Minnesota, which President Donald Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there. Abbott directs ‘bad lawyers’ comment at Minnesota attorney general After the judge’s decision, Ellison posted online that the Texas governor had an obligation to extradite Castro. And by refusing to extradite him, “Greg Abbott is turning Texas into a sanctuary state for violent criminals.” Abbott responded to Ellison. “You guys are such bad lawyers. You showed up unprepared, uninformed & unpersuasive,” Abbott wrote online. “You don’t know the law & it showed.” The Texas governor accused Minnesota of refusing to enforce immigration laws and threatened to send immigrants in the future to their state as he did with New York City, when thousands were released into Texas under President Joe Biden’s administration. A message seeking reaction from Ellison was sent to his office Thursday. Minnesota officials say Castro could flee the country, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico, talking “about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released,” according to the lawsuit. The judge conceded that Castro could flee the country but added that “the threat of injury by itself does not create an issue ripe for adjudication.”

articles.title: Thieves stole 400,000 juvenile oysters worth about $350,000 from an Australian farm; the grower says a third of his stock is gone and the theft has set him back two to three years
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Waterborne thieves have raided an oyster farm on the New South Wales Mid North Coast, stealing 400,000 young oysters worth about $350,000 AUD (£177,00.
articles.body: Waterborne thieves have raided an oyster farm on the New South Wales Mid North Coast, stealing 400,000 young oysters worth about $350,000 AUD (£177,000). The theft has wiped out around a third of the grower's total stock. The large-scale theft is being investigated by the New South Wales Police Force. It happened at a remote water lease operated by Latitude 31 Oysters at Scotts Creek on Oxley Island, along the Manning River near Old Bar. According to ABC News Australia, farm owner Ryan Freeman discovered the theft on Tuesday morning, 25 August 2026, when he arrived to prepare his stock for the upcoming Christmas sales season. The thieves removed about 320 mesh bags containing young Sydney rock oysters, as well as floating equipment and sorting gear. Freeman said the total loss, including damaged equipment and stolen hardware, could be as high as $400,000 AUD. "We noticed our floating gear and tumblers were missing," Freeman said while inspecting the oyster leases. The theft comes at a critical time for the business. About 80 per cent of the stolen oysters were due to be harvested and sold before Christmas. The farm usually supplies between 35,000 and 40,000 dozen oysters to Australian markets during the festive season.Major financial loss and delaysSydney rock oysters take about three years to reach market size. Freeman said the theft could therefore set his business back by two to three years. Losing a third of his total stock also means there is little time to replace the young oysters before the immediate production cycle. Rebuilding the lost stock will take years. Detectives from the New South Wales Police Force and local rural crime investigators believe the theft would have required good knowledge of the river, a suitable boat and several people working together to remove hundreds of heavy bags without being noticed. Police have appealed to local residents, boat owners and other river users for information. They are asking anyone who saw suspicious boats or activity around Scotts Creek to contact authorities. The incident has also raised concerns about agricultural crime in Australia's aquaculture industry, where valuable seafood can be an attractive target for thieves.Possible industry knowledgeIndustry figures believe the timing and scale of the theft could indicate that the criminals knew how the oyster farm operated and understood the layout of the river. Gary Rodley, owner of Tathra Oysters on the NSW South Coast, told ABC News Australia that mature Sydney rock oysters can sell for between $1.50 and $2.00 AUD each at wholesale prices. He said the targeted nature of the theft suggested that someone familiar with commercial oyster farming could have been involved. "They're a rare oyster that only grow up and down the New South Wales coastline, so they're a very, very small percentage of the world's oyster crop," Rodley said. "It's regarded as probably the best flavoured oyster in the world by a lot of people – they're a very flavoursome oyster and highly regarded as a table oyster that's eaten natural. That's a particular set of circumstances that a lot of people value highly." A Manning River oyster farmer, who spoke anonymously, said local growers were already facing serious problems after major floods in 2021 and 2025. Those floods destroyed large amounts of oyster stock across several regional river systems and contributed to a shortage of market-ready Sydney rock oysters across eastern Australia. "The worst case scenario is it could be someone within the industry that has had a shortfall, who has gone past that area of the river and knows it only gets used certain times of year, and they've gone 'they'll never know until they get back'," the grower said.More pressure on oyster farmersThe loss of 400,000 young oysters from the Manning River comes as Australian shellfish farmers face higher fuel costs, biosecurity concerns and increasingly unpredictable weather. The shortage of Sydney rock oysters has pushed up farm-gate prices, making floating oyster leases more attractive to criminals. Unlike land farms, which can be protected by fences and gates, oyster farms are spread across public rivers and estuaries. The leases are usually marked with floating signs and equipment. Some larger farms have installed solar-powered security cameras and GPS trackers on their equipment. However, keeping watch over large and isolated waterways, especially at night, remains difficult for smaller family businesses. New South Wales Police said the investigation is continuing through specialised rural crime teams. Officers are reviewing marine transport records and checking regional seafood supply chains. Police have also urged anyone offered large or suspicious quantities of Sydney rock oysters without proper paperwork showing their legal source to report it immediately.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Jellyfish force partial shutdown of France's Gravelines nuclear plant
articles.summary: It is the second consecutive year that jellyfish has forced the closure of the Gravelines power station in northern France.
articles.body:
A massive influx of jellyfish has led to the partial shutdown of a nuclear reactor in northern France.

Two of Gravelines nuclear power station's six units were shut down on Wednesday and Thursday because of the presence of jellyfish in the seawater filtration system, which is used for cooling, Électricité de France (EDF) said.

A third unit has been shut down since 10 August due to the same issue, while a fourth has been closed for an inspection.

Gravelines, one of the country's biggest nuclear power stations located between Dunkirk and Calais in the Hauts-de-France region, was also closed last August because of jellyfish in its filters.

EDF said that units three, four and six were now shut.

Unit three had only been reconnected to the grid on 18 August after the first wave of jellyfish earlier this month, the company said, while units one and two were also operating at reduced power as a preventative measure.

Gravelines' six units each produce 900 megawatts of power. The station is cooled from a canal connected to the North Sea.

Several species of jellyfish are native and can be seen around the coast when the waters are warm.

Jellyfish are at their most active in the warmer months. Hot weather increases plankton levels at the water's surface, drawing jellyfish up, experts say.

Measures have been implemented to try to prevent jellyfish infiltration, including a partnership with fishermen who capture and release them further offshore, according to French outlet Ici.

There have been similar issues at other nuclear stations, including at the Torness plant in Scotland in 2011 and Sweden's Oskarshamn plant in 2013, but such cases are rare.

articles.title: Cyberattack hits 3 UK airports, data of 8.7m customers leaked; spokesperson says 'no operational disruption'
articles.summary: UK News: A serious cyberattack on Manchester, London Stansted, and East Midlands airports has compromised the personal information of 8.7 million customers, sparking warnings from airport authorities. While operations remain unaffected, customers are advised to be vigilant against potential scams.
articles.body: The UK's three major airports Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands have been hit by a cyber-attack. Hackers accessed the personal data of about 8.7 million customers, The Guardian reported.Manchester Airports Group (MAG), which operates all three airports, said the compromised information included customers’ email addresses, phone numbers, vehicle registration numbers and postcodes. The affected data was linked to car park, lounge and fast-track bookings, as well as in-airport Wi-Fi sign-ups.MAG said the incident did not affect passenger safety or aviation security and caused no disruption to airport operations. It also said the affected system did not contain customers’ bank or payment details.The company said the incident occurred over the weekend and that it had “immediately contained the risk”. MAG is working with specialist advisers and taking steps to protect its systems and customer information.“We have informed and are working with the relevant authorities,” a MAG spokesperson said on Thursday. “At no point has passenger safety or aviation security been compromised.”The spokesperson said the incident had “not resulted in any operational disruption”, adding that airport operations remained unaffected and customer parking services continued to operate normally.MAG also apologised to customers for any concern caused by the incident and said it takes the security of customer information “extremely seriously”.London Stansted separately warned customers to be alert to possible follow-up attempts by scammers using the stolen information.In an email to customers, the airport urged them to be particularly cautious of unexpected emails, phone calls or text messages claiming to be from the airport.“We will never contact you unexpectedly to ask for payment or banking information,” the email said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: More than 100 years ago, red mangroves were introduced to Hawaii; now crews are trying to eradicate them from nearly 2 miles of waterways to restore wetlands and protect endangered birds
articles.summary: US News: Environmental teams in Hawaii have launched a major effort to remove invasive red mangroves from nearly two miles of waterways in Kailua. The project .
articles.body: Environmental teams in Hawaii have launched a major effort to remove invasive red mangroves from nearly two miles of waterways in Kailua. The project aims to reverse more than a century of environmental damage and protect endangered native waterbirds. The multi-year project, announced on 25 August 2026 by the Hawaii Department of Land and Natural Resources (DLNR), will target thick stands of red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle) that have spread through streams feeding the Kawainui and Hamakua wetlands on the windward coast of Oahu. The work is funded through joint grants from the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). It brings together the DLNR Division of Forestry and Wildlife (DOFAW), the University of Hawaii Pacific Cooperative Studies Unit and Kailua-based environmental non-profit Hui o Koolaupoko (HOK). Community involvement is a key part of the plan. Project leaders are asking volunteers, community groups, schools and private landowners to help field crews remove young mangrove plants and seed pods from affected waterways. The first physical removal work is scheduled to begin on Saturday, 26 September 2026. Crews will initially focus on Kawainui Stream between Kawainui Neighborhood Park and the Hamakua Street Bridge.An invasive tree that changed Hawaii's wetlandsRed mangroves are not native to the Hawaiian Islands. The trees were first brought from Florida to Molokai in 1902 by the American Sugar Company to help control coastal erosion and soil runoff. They later spread quickly through brackish estuaries, coastal lagoons and freshwater streams across the islands. Over more than a century, the invasive trees have changed the way water moves through wetlands. Unlike native Hawaiian coastal plants, red mangroves grow dense networks of stilt roots that trap sediment, raise stream beds, slow water flow and reduce water quality. In low-lying areas such as Kailua, blocked drainage can also increase the risk of local flooding during periods of heavy rain. Ecologists say the changes have seriously damaged important wetland habitats. Thick mangrove canopies push out native plants and remove open mudflats that provide important feeding and nesting areas for endangered Hawaiian waterbirds. Birds affected by the spread of mangroves include the Hawaiian stilt (aeo), Hawaiian coot (alae keokeo), Hawaiian gallinule (alae ula) and Hawaiian duck (koloa maoli). These birds depend on shallow, open water and clear views to spot predators such as mongooses and feral cats.Community support is keyField teams will remove small trees and seed pods before planting native Hawaiian wetland species along cleared stream banks. Native plants can help hold the soil in place and reduce the chances of mangrove seedlings becoming established again. Organisers say long-term community support will be essential because the project covers both public and private land along the waterways. “We're honored to partner with the Division of Forestry and Wildlife to bring the wetland and bird habitat restoration techniques we've developed at Heʻeia State Park back to our hometown,” said Kristen Nalani Kane, Executive Director of Hui o Koolaupoko, in an official statement released by the DLNR. “This is the first of many phases needed to achieve functional eradication of mangrove from Kailua's waterways, and community participation will be essential to its long-term success.”Scientists involved in the project said restoring the natural flow of water will benefit the wider ecosystem, not just native birds. “Removing invasive mangrove is essential to restoring the health and function of these wetlands. This project reflects what's possible when agencies and community work together to create better habitat for Hawaiʻi's native waterbirds and a more resilient ecosystem for future generations,” said Lailan Uy, a wetland biologist working with the University of Hawaii Pacific Cooperative Studies Unit in cooperation with state wildlife authorities.Long-term work neededThe Kailua project builds on earlier restoration efforts at nearby Heeia State Park and the Kawainui Marsh State Wildlife Sanctuary, the largest remaining wetland on Oahu. Removing mangroves is only the first step. Long-term monitoring will be needed because mature trees can produce hundreds of pencil-shaped seed pods called propagules. These can float for long distances on ocean currents and tides before taking root in muddy areas. Without regular checks and removal of new seedlings, cleared areas can quickly become covered by mangroves again. Monthly community workdays are planned from late 2026 through 2027, with participation focused on people aged 18 and older. Hui o Koolaupoko coordinators are also working with private landowners along the streams to provide access to removal crews and help ensure the full two-mile area is covered. By restoring natural water flow and bringing back open mudflat habitats, conservationists hope to make Oahu's windward coast more resilient to climate change while creating safer habitats for some of Hawaii's unique native species.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Humanoid robot outruns Usain Bolt record as China races ahead
articles.summary: X-Humanoid's TianGong Ultra ran 100 meters in 9.32 seconds at Beijing's World Humanoid Robot Games, beating last year's winner by more than half.
articles.body: If your mental image of a humanoid robot still involves stiff knees and awkward demos, you may want to update it. A Chinese humanoid robot has now covered 100 meters faster than Usain Bolt's 9.58-second human world record. At the opening of Beijing's World Humanoid Robot Games, an X-Humanoid robot completed the 100-meter sprint in 9.39 seconds. Then the number dropped again. X-Humanoid announced on Aug. 25 that TianGong Ultra ultimately posted a 9.32-second time during the competition. The company says its robots reset the mark several times during roughly two hours of racing. Before anybody starts rewriting the Olympic record books, keep some perspective. Bolt still holds the official men's 100-meter world record recognized by World Athletics. These robots compete under their own rules in a separate event. CHINESE ROBOT BREAKS HUMAN WORLD RECORD IN BEIJING HALF-MARATHON Still, look at how quickly this technology is moving. For me, the bigger story goes far beyond a robot beating Bolt's time. We are watching humanoid machines go from clumsy demonstrations to increasingly capable physical systems at remarkable speed. THIS SATURDAY! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward. Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com. Humanoid robots are suddenly getting very fast The second World Humanoid Robot Games opened Aug. 22 at Beijing's National Speed Skating Oval, known as the Ice Ribbon, and ran through Aug. 26. Organizers registered 666 teams and 2,056 robots for this year's event. The competition included 51 events and 1,301 competition sessions. The robots compete in track and field events along with challenges designed around real-world jobs. Organizers have also added tests involving physical skills such as weightlifting and tug of war. That mix tells you something about what China wants these machines to become. The Games give developers a place to push speed and strength. They also expose weaknesses that can be harder to see in a carefully edited demonstration video. TianGong Ultra ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds, then 9.32 The first number that grabbed worldwide attention was 9.39 seconds. That was already quicker than Bolt's 9.58-second human record from 2009. The comparison spread fast because almost everyone understands what a 100-meter sprint represents. Then X-Humanoid released its updated results. The company says TianGong Ultra eventually reached 9.32 seconds, while other X-Humanoid teams recorded times of 9.34, 9.38 and 9.39 seconds. The exact comparison with Bolt needs context. These robots do not start, run or stop under the same conditions as human Olympic athletes. However, that does not make the improvement meaningless. A humanoid staying upright at that speed requires serious coordination between its motors, balance system, sensors and software. All of those pieces have to work together while the machine continuously adjusts its body. That is what catches my attention. Last year's winner took more than twice as long The rate of improvement becomes even clearer when you look back only one year. At the inaugural World Humanoid Robot Games in 2025, the winning 100-meter robot finished in 21.50 seconds. Now robots from the same development ecosystem are running the distance in less than 10 seconds. That is an enormous leap in a short period. We have already been following this acceleration at CyberGuy. Earlier this year, we showed you a Chinese humanoid called Bolt that reached 22 mph during testing. Running fast looks impressive on video. Yet the technology underneath that speed could become useful in places far removed from a racetrack. A robot also jumped about 9 feet 5 inches Running was only part of the show. An X-Humanoid robot reached 2.88 meters, or about 9 feet 5 inches, in a standing high jump. That height exceeds the recognized men's high jump world record of 2.45 meters, or about 8 feet, set by Cuba's Javier Sotomayor in 1993. Again, we need context. Sotomayor's world record came from a conventional high jump with a running approach. The robot competed in a standing high jump. Those events use very different mechanics. So the robot did not erase Sotomayor from the record books. What it did demonstrate was impressive explosive power and body control from a humanoid machine. Those capabilities could eventually translate into something far more useful than clearing a bar. ROBOT LEARNS TO DISMANTLE BROKEN MACHINES Once robots can move like this, you start asking where they can go A fast humanoid robot does not need to become a track star to become valuable. Better mobility could help a robot move through a disaster area where sending a person could be dangerous. A machine that stays balanced while carrying equipment could eventually handle physically demanding jobs. Then you start thinking about environments where people would rather avoid going altogether. That brings us to the part of this story that deserves much more attention. One developer at the Games believes humanoid robot soldiers could arrive within the next decade. One developer predicts robot soldiers within 5 to 10 years Robotics engineer Yang Kun, who works for Shanghai-based humanoid robotics company AG BOT, says that he believes Chinese companies could be only five to 10 years away from robot soldiers. His company's A3 humanoid competed in kickboxing at the Games. Yang described military and combat use as part of where he believes humanoid robotics could eventually go. That prediction deserves context. This comes from one developer. It does not represent an announced Chinese government timetable for deploying humanoid soldiers. I would not take five to 10 years as gospel. Technology forecasts can move quickly in either direction. A machine can perform beautifully in a controlled environment and then struggle once the surroundings become unpredictable. What I would pay attention to is where developers believe this technology is headed. When people building these machines start discussing military applications, that tells us the conversation has already moved far beyond robots entertaining crowds at sporting events. A battlefield would expose everything robots still struggle with Running fast in a straight line is one challenge. Navigating a damaged building while carrying equipment presents an entirely different problem. A robot may encounter unstable ground, blocked paths and people moving unpredictably around it. Then comes the far harder issue of decision-making. A sprint gives a robot a clear destination. Real life rarely does. Military environments make that problem even tougher because communication can disappear without warning. Sensors can misread a situation. Software may face circumstances developers never anticipated. That is why I would keep some perspective when watching these record-setting performances. The robots are getting impressive. They also still fall down. At the Games, some fast-running robots had trouble stopping after crossing the finish line and crashed into padded barriers. That creates a pretty good visual reminder of the gap between raw speed and reliable control. China is testing robots for real-world jobs too The organizers appear very aware of that gap. This year, Beijing upgraded the 100-meter event so robots must compete fully autonomously. Scenario-based events also encourage autonomous positioning, recognition and operation. The robots also face tasks inside settings modeled after factories, hotels and homes. Emergency-response challenges push them into situations where they must interact with their surroundings for longer periods. That part interests me even more than a sprint record. A robot that runs 100 meters in nine seconds creates a great headline. A robot that can reliably work for hours without somebody constantly guiding it could change entire industries. China appears focused on both. CyberGuy has also reported on efforts to scale humanoid manufacturing in China, with factories preparing to build thousands of machines. That brings us to the larger technology race. UNITREE G1 HUMANOID ROBOT ICE SKATES AND ROLLERBLADES The U.S.-China tech race now has arms and legs We hear constantly about competition between the United States and China over artificial intelligence. Humanoid robotics adds a physical layer to that race. The country that develops powerful artificial intelligence gains one advantage. The country that can put that intelligence inside a reliable robot body and manufacture those machines at scale could gain something much larger. Suddenly, the software can move through the physical world. It can enter an industrial facility. It can cross dangerous terrain or potentially operate where sending people would carry significant risk. U.S. regulators are already treating advanced foreign robotics as a national-security concern. On July 28, the Federal Communications Commission added foreign-produced advanced robotic devices to its Covered List. The category includes qualifying humanoid robots and other advanced mobile robotic systems. The change means covered new devices generally cannot receive the FCC equipment authorization required for import or sale in the United States unless they receive an applicable conditional approval. That tells you Washington sees connected robots as more than another gadget category. The AI brain could become the bigger story For years, humanoid developers faced a frustrating mechanical challenge. How do you make a two-legged machine move efficiently without constantly falling over? Engineers still have plenty of work ahead. Yet today's machines move very differently from the awkward humanoids we watched only a few years ago. That changes what developers can focus on next. As robot bodies become faster and stronger, artificial intelligence continues improving at the same time. A more capable body could perform difficult physical work. Better AI could help that machine understand what it sees and determine what to do next. Put those advances together and humanoids become much more interesting. We recently showed you another humanoid demonstrating impressive running and movement skills. The biggest hurdle now may become less about making a robot move and more about making sure it makes good decisions once it gets there. What this means to you You probably will not see a humanoid robot soldier walking down your street anytime soon. You may encounter the technology behind these machines much sooner. The balance system that keeps a robot upright during a sprint could help one move through rubble after an earthquake. More capable sensors could allow robots to operate around human workers more safely. Factories will likely remain one of the first major targets. Most buildings and workplaces were designed around the human body. That makes humanoids appealing because companies could potentially deploy them without rebuilding every workspace around a specialized machine. As reliability improves and costs come down, those capabilities could expand into other areas. The military discussion raises much harder questions. How much decision-making authority should an autonomous machine have? Who carries responsibility if an AI-controlled robot makes a dangerous mistake? Those conversations should happen before the machines become capable enough to force them. Because the technology is moving quickly. Kurt's key takeaways The Bolt comparison grabs your attention, but the bigger story for me is how quickly humanoid robots are becoming more capable. A 9.39-second 100-meter run shows how fast the motors, balance systems and software are improving. The military angle deserves attention too. One Chinese robotics engineer predicts robot soldiers could arrive within five to 10 years. I would not treat that timeline as gospel, but it shows where some developers believe this technology is headed. For America, this is another front in the technology race with China. A country that can combine advanced AI with reliable robot bodies and produce large numbers of them could gain a major advantage. We also need perspective. Running fast on a controlled track is far easier than navigating an unpredictable environment and making safe decisions. What I am watching now is how quickly these stronger robot bodies advance alongside increasingly capable AI. If humanoid robots can outrun us, carry heavy equipment and make more decisions on their own, where would you draw the line on how much power we should give them? articles.title: Mystery Iron Age fort in Shropshire excavated after 40 years as archaeologists investigate its strange wetlands, huge earthworks and unexplained causeways
articles.summary: UK News: An unusual Iron Age fort hidden in the former wetlands of Shropshire is being excavated again after almost four decades, giving archaeologists a rare .
articles.body: An unusual Iron Age fort hidden in the former wetlands of Shropshire is being excavated again after almost four decades, giving archaeologists a rare opportunity to investigate one of Britain’s most enigmatic lowland forts. Wall Camp, near Kynnersley and Telford, has been selected as the new home of the University of Birmingham’s Archaeology Field School under a 10-year research partnership. More than 60 students joined academics for the first three-week excavation in June 2026, opening three trenches across the Scheduled Monument. The project is examining the fort’s banks, ditches, entrance and unusual internal layout, including causeways that appear to lead nowhere. The University of Birmingham, which announced the excavation on 23 July, says the site is among the largest and best-preserved examples of a low-lying “marsh fort” in Britain.Why is Wall Camp such an unusual Iron Age fort?Wall Camp stands in an unexpected setting for an Iron Age fort. Rather than occupying a prominent hilltop, it was constructed on a slightly raised island within the Weald Moors, an area that was once characterised by boggy woodland and wetlands. The fort is surrounded by as many as five concentric earthworks, creating an imposing and complex defensive landscape across the low-lying terrain. The University of Birmingham describes it as one of Britain’s largest and best-preserved examples of a marsh fort, a comparatively rare type of monument. The monument covers roughly 12 hectares and has long challenged straightforward interpretations. Earlier archaeological work established Iron Age occupation, but questions remain over why such substantial earthworks were constructed in a wetland environment. Historic England’s Heritage Gateway records Wall Camp as a large, complex Iron Age defended settlement that originally stood on an island in fenland.What are archaeologists looking for in the new Wall Camp excavation?The first modern campaign is designed to answer some of the most basic questions about how Wall Camp functioned. The team opened three trenches during a three-week excavation, focusing on the site’s layout, architecture, banks, ditches and elaborate entranceway. Researchers are particularly interested in understanding how people moved into and out of the fort and why its unusual features were positioned where they are. Among the most puzzling features are several causeways that appear to lead nowhere. Their purpose remains uncertain, and the excavation could establish whether they were practical routes, carefully designed approaches or structures connected with activities beyond conventional settlement. The project is being led by Dr Theo Reeves, Professor Henry Chapman and Dr David Smith, with Historic England involved in the wider research.“The site is a fascinating Iron Age fort with many intriguing features, and it will be wonderful to examine them up close,” says Professor Henry Chapman. The University also says the 10-year partnership will allow successive student cohorts to combine archaeological training with continuing investigation of the monument.What has already been discovered at Wall Camp?Although the latest excavation marks the first major return to Wall Camp in about 40 years, archaeologists already know that the site contains evidence of substantial Iron Age activity. Earlier excavations uncovered roundhouses and pottery associated with regional salt-trading networks. A particularly striking discovery was a rare blue glass bead established as an example of exceptional craftsmanship. These finds indicate that Wall Camp was connected to wider networks rather than being an isolated monument. The site has also produced evidence that complicates its interpretation. Archaeological records show Iron Age pottery and structures within the fort, while radiocarbon and artefactual evidence places occupation broadly between the third century BC and the first century AD. The surrounding wetland may have been equally important. Earlier research has considered possibilities ranging from settlement and pastoral activity to high-status, refuge or ritual functions, reflecting how little is still known about the monument’s precise role.Will the new excavation finally solve Wall Camp’s Iron Age mystery?The latest excavation is only the first stage of a much larger investigation into Wall Camp. According to the University of Birmingham, the new field school forms part of a 10-year research collaboration that will allow archaeologists to return to the site repeatedly and build a much fuller picture of how the fort developed and was used. The June 2026 excavation focused on understanding its layout, entrance, banks, ditches and unusual access features, particularly causeways that appear to lead nowhere. Researchers now want to establish when Wall Camp was constructed, why such enormous earthworks were built and what purpose the surrounding wetlands served. The answers could reveal whether the marshland was simply a defensive advantage or played a deeper economic, social or ceremonial role. Historic England notes that the ditches and buried surfaces may preserve waterlogged organic material capable of revealing changes in the local environment and land use. The excavation could therefore do more than uncover artefacts, it may ultimately explain why this unusual Iron Age monument was built in such an extraordinary landscape.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
