articles.title: RANDOM MUSING | How Zohran Mamdani mastered Donald Trump's 'Art of the Deal'
articles.summary: US News: Interestingly, Donald Trump laid down 11 rules for successful deal-making in The Art of the Deal. Mamdani’s first eight months as mayor suggest that he has followed Trump’s rules more faithfully than most people who actually work for Trump.
articles.body: Every generation has technological habits that confuse the next. Recording TV shows on a thing called a VCR. Sending free SMSes from a bootleg site. Burning CDs. Downloading wallpapers on Santa Banta. Each chore sounds arcanely archaic to the next generation.And the chances are that if you grew up in the early noughties and developed a taste for English music to fit in with anglicised Macaulayputras, you downloaded songs from illegal torrent sites before playing them on Winamp. You might have sung along to how it no longer matters, tried to memorise the lyrics to Lose Yourself (What comes after “Mom’s spaghetti”?) and definitely knew that space may be the final frontier, but it’s made in a Hollywood basement. And much like that, Zohran Mamdani feels like he was conceived in a left-liberal lab to tick all the boxes.The New York mayor is a gallimaufry of values global progressives hold dear: being anti-Israel, being anti-Hindu, being anti-rich, underperforming in SAT exams, trying to pass oneself off as a different race and blaming one’s problems on everyone but oneself.But Mamdani has managed something that none of his progressive peers has: winning while paying the mildest obeisance to the values that his various constituencies hold dear. And he does it while complaining about things without giving the impression of being bitter.Of course, he’s aided and abetted by a mainstream press that waxes lyrical about him as though he’s the second coming of Obama and never gets pushback about his mendacities. For example, during a debate between New York mayoral hopefuls, he claimed that Muslims don’t even exist in Gujarat, an obvious mendacity that would have been called out if it had come from a white politician wearing a red cap. But then again, Kamala Harris has claimed that her grandfather was an Indian freedom fighter, despite his having been part of the Imperial Civil Service under the Crown, and not one American publication has fact-checked her. Those checks are reserved only for Tucker Carlson and white people wearing red caps.But Zohran is exceptionally good at what critics call virtue-signalling but smart people know is making the right noise. Take his smart and masterful handling of the RSS chief’s upcoming event at Madison Square Garden, where he made his mild disdain known before pointing out that it was a private event and he couldn’t do anything to stop it. It was the kind of political manoeuvring that has seen him become the only Democrat who has been able to get more than a fair shake out of Donald Trump.The RSS manoeuvre contained Mamdani’s method in miniature. He gave his progressive supporters the condemnation they wanted, acknowledged that the organisers had the right to hold a private event and ensured that City Hall would not be held responsible for stopping something it had no power to stop. Everyone received something from the deal, especially Mamdani.Interestingly, Donald Trump laid down 11 rules for successful deal-making in The Art of the Deal. Mamdani’s first eight months as mayor suggest that he has followed Trump’s rules more faithfully than most people who actually work for Trump.Rule 1: Think bigMamdani’s campaign was full of big promises to turn the Big Apple into a utopia of affordable homes, parks, schools and union jobs. The minor hitch is that it needs money from a federal government headed by a man he labelled a “despot” and “fascist”. That didn’t stop Mamdani from smiling into Trump’s embrace with a fake New York Daily News header and the promise of something Trump had coveted long before he became POTUS: love from New York. The money might or might not arrive, but Mamdani did get Trump to release an ICE detainee, which shows that he has completely understood Trump’s maxim of thinking big.Rule 2: Protect the downside and the upside will take care of itselfThis is easier said than done, but Mamdani managed it by retaining NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch, who also happens to be a billionaire heiress. This allowed him to distance himself from the politically charged “Defund the Police” chant and even claim credit for major crime and murder rates falling by 5.8% and 24.7% in the first six months of 2026. Mamdani did the same with the Israel Day Parade, appearing with Tisch to announce security for it while staying away, so Palestinians got the boycott they wanted while Jewish New Yorkers received the protection. The art of being present yet absent would have made Schrödinger smile.Rule 3: Maximise your optionsIn Game of Thrones, Cersei Lannister explained to Littlefinger: “Power is power.” And it’s something Mamdani has learnt well. He opposed mayoral control of New York’s public schools but, hours after taking office, reversed course, asked Albany to extend mayoral control and appointed his chancellor.Mamdani promised to use the system more democratically than his predecessors because ending it might have satisfied his progressive supporters but would have surrendered a powerful lever. Instead, he explained to parents that he was in charge.Rule 4: Know your marketNew Yorkers are, perhaps after Indians, the most politically disagreeable people on a vast number of topics, from Gaza and policing to whether Colin Jost should be dropped from SNL, but they all agree that rent is too high. Whatever happens in other parts of the world is secondary.In June, the Rent Guidelines Board, dominated by Mamdani appointees, voted 7-1 to freeze rents on one-year and two-year leases covering roughly one million rent-stabilised apartments. Now, landlords warn that this will lead to wear and tear, reduce maintenance and make the situation worse, but tenants vastly outnumber landlords and, in a democracy, populism, not economic logic, always wins.Rule 5: Use your leverageEvery politician knows that you can’t always get what you want, but if you try hard enough, you will get what you need. Mamdani demanded $5.5 billion from Albany through higher taxes on corporations, warning that failure could force a 9.5% property-tax hike in New York. Governor Kathy Hochul refused but eventually gave enough fiscal help for Mamdani to withdraw the threat, allowing both to declare victory. Many years ago, American scholar Stephen P. Cohen said that Pakistan negotiates with the world by holding a gun to its own head, and while Mamdani might have descended from this side of the border, he showed that you can use leverage with a hint of self-sabotage.Rule 6: Enhance your locationTrump argued that “location, location, location” was misunderstood. A real-estate developer didn’t need the best address, only the best deal, and that could be done with promotion and psychology. He often cited Trump Plaza on Third Avenue as an example.Mamdani appears to have used that logic for municipal groceries, and instead of paying New York’s astronomical rents, the city will place five stores in publicly owned properties, with the city covering rent and property taxes. Unfair to existing grocers? Sure, but that’s how one changes the game and gives the appearance of change without making a real change.Rule 7: Get the word outLong before the attention economy came around, Donald Trump wrote that the greatest product in the world is worthless if nobody knows about it. A tree falling in a forest with no observer makes no noise. That’s one piece of advice that took Mamdani from a virtual unknown to being dubbed the “Everywhere Mayor” by The New Yorker.He appears on reels, streets and Taxi TV, while his Office of Mass Engagement carries his campaign machinery into City Hall. Budgets become explainers, potholes become videos and municipal announcements become content. Most mayors govern and then publicise. Mamdani governs through publicity, ensuring New Yorkers encounter him even when they are trying to hail a cab.Rule 8: Fight backRule 8 is perhaps the one rule that Trump has mastered himself, after facing the full onslaught of America’s four estates for four years before making a comeback to the White House. Mamdani has found his opponent in Amazon, an organisation that makes LuthorCorp look like a mum-and-pop store, through the Delivery Protection Act. This would impose employment and safety rules on warehouses and give Mamdani the pantomime Lex Luthor he needs to keep his base happy.Rule 9: Deliver the goodsNow, this one is open to interpretation as America carries on its never-ending war on Iran under Trump, who appears to have interpreted “goods” as bombs and never-ending ceasefire agreements. Mamdani has opted for parcels. In his first 100 days, the administration secured $9.3 million in restitution for workers, including settlements that produced $5 million for delivery workers. The buses aren’t free and the groceries might not work, but Mamdani has delivered enough “goods” to keep New Yorkers from asking when the rest of the order will arrive.Rule 10: Contain the costsNow, this isn’t a precept the Trump administration follows anymore, given its vacillating trade wars and tariffs. Mamdani, however, discovered fiscal conservatism when the City Council approved one-time payments of up to $10,000 for school paraprofessionals at a cost exceeding $300 million.Despite campaigning with the teachers’ union and promising better pay, Mamdani allowed the measure to become law without signing it and then sued to block it, arguing that it had bypassed collective bargaining.Ergo, a socialist mayor is fighting a union-backed payment to low-paid workers in defence of collective bargaining. Otto von Bismarck would have heartily approved because politics is, after all, the art of the possible.Rule 11: Have funFinally, Mamdani has definitely followed the last rule of Trump’s playbook by looking like the only progressive having fun in the era of Trump. While his reels and social-media game have always been top-drawer, even his teams are performing miracles. Mamdani is now basking in the afterglow of what The Athletic has named “Mamdani’s Sports Summer”, much to the chagrin of Fox acolytes, who are fuming about the Mamdani Effect. But sports fandom runs on superstitions, and Mamdani’s ascent has seen Arsenal win the league for the first time since 2004 and the Knicks win the NBA championship for the first time since 1973.As the Bengali poet MD Ahnaf Hossain, whose art is now being compared to Rabindranath Tagore and Kazi Nazrul Islam, chanted: “My mayor’s Muslim, my bagel’s Jewish, the Pope’s on our side, Knicks in five.”Trump might have written The Art of the Deal, but at this moment, it looks as though it is Zohran Mamdani who is living up to it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Tropical Storm Dolly forms in the Atlantic and could bring heavy rain to parts of the Caribbean
articles.summary: Tropical Storm Dolly formed Thursday in the Atlantic Ocean far from land, and forecasters said it could bring heavy rain to portions of the Caribbean.
articles.body: MIAMI — Tropical Storm Dolly formed Thursday in the Atlantic Ocean far from land, and forecasters said it could bring heavy rain to portions of the Caribbean. The storm was about 1,555 miles (2,500 kilometers) east of the Leeward Islands and had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (64 kph), the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said. Dolly was moving west. The storm and its name had no connection to Dolly Parton’s death Tuesday. Storm systems are named by procedures set by the World Meteorological Organization, and the lists of names are reused every six years. For the Atlantic region, the lists are alphabetical and alternate male and female names. Dolly was the fourth named storm for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season. There were no coastal watches or warnings in effect, but the center said the Leeward Islands could get heavy rain Saturday and Sunday. The Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and Hispaniola could see heavy rain Sunday and Monday. Little change in strength is forecast during the coming days, the center said, but flash flooding could occur. The Atlantic hurricane season started with Tropical Storm Arthur coming ashore on the U.S. Gulf Coast in June, and Tropical Storm Bertha dumped rain in Louisiana and Texas in July. Tropical Storm Cristobal formed and quickly dissipated in the Atlantic earlier in August. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has forecast a below-average Atlantic hurricane season due to El Nino. It forecast eight to 14 named storms, with three to six of them reaching hurricane strength and one to three of those intensifying to major hurricanes. The NHC and other weather agencies name storms to easily communicate warnings about them to people and to avoid confusion. The WMO says names are chosen to be short, easy to pronounce and familiar to the regions of the world where the storm names are used. It meets regularly to evaluate potential names, and some names are retired for reasons of sensitivity, particularly for deadly or destructive storms. One name from the 2025 season was retired, Melissa, which was a Category 5 hurricane that brought devastation to the Caribbean.

articles.title: Man dies after vehicle gets stranded in Death Valley, attempts trek across blistering salt flats
articles.summary: A French tourist became stranded in California's Death Valley National Park in scorching heat after his vehicle got stuck in mud near Badwater Basin and he tried to walk out.
articles.body: A French tourist died this month after becoming stranded in California's Death Valley National Park amid sweltering temperatures. The National Park Service (NPS) announced the death of Pierre Michel Formosa, 68, on Aug. 21. Park officials said Formosa and his travel companion, also a French national, were driving on West Side Road along the Badwater Basin on Aug. 17 when their vehicle "became stuck in mud." NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING' "With no other vehicles in the area, the men began walking across the salt flats toward Badwater Road to seek assistance," park officials said. Temperatures were as high as 116°F — and eventually Formosa was "unable to continue." Formosa's companion continued on and eventually was helped by a passing motorist — who alerted officials at the Furnace Creek Visitor Center at around 2 p.m. NPS rangers soon began searching for Formosa, along with an Inyo County sheriff’s deputy. YELLOWSTONE OFFICIALS DECIDE FATE OF BISON THAT LAUNCHED GRANDFATHER 8 FEET IN AIR A California Highway Patrol helicopter later joined the search and found Formosa later that afternoon, about 1.5 miles from Badwater Road. "He was pronounced dead at the scene," NPS officials said. "The Inyo County coroner will determine the cause and manner of death." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER In a statement, Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds said he was "grateful to everyone who took part in the search, and our thoughts are with his loved ones." "This is a heartbreaking reminder of how quickly conditions here can turn dangerous," said Reynolds. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Death Valley is an extraordinary place, but its heat, distances and remoteness can be dangerous, regardless of experience." Fox News Digital reached out to Death Valley National Park and the Inyo County Sheriff's Office for additional information. Earlier this summer, an 18-year-old hiker died after experiencing heat-related symptoms while hiking the Grand Canyon's popular Bright Angel Trail, according to the NPS. articles.title: Inverness Castle facing a loss of almost £1.4m in first year
articles.summary: Highland councillors have been told tickets sales are lower than expected.
articles.body:
The new Inverness Castle Experience is set to make a financial loss of almost £1.4m this year because of lower than expected ticket sales.

The tourist attraction, which features an interactive journey through Highland history and culture, is getting about half the number of projected visitors.

The castle, a former sheriff court, officially opened to visitors in February following a transformation project costing about £47m.

A meeting of Highland Council's corporate resources committee heard that a new five-year strategy was being developed by the operators, Highlife Highland, to support its long-term success.

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

There have been just over 80,000 paying visitors so far this year.

Highlife Highland, which operates Highland Council-owned leisure and sports venues, said that was about 55% of the projected figure.

Lower than expected footfall has led to fewer sales in the castle's shop and food and drink outlets.

In a presentation Highlife Highland's chief executive Steve Walsh said staffing levels had already been reduced and they had moved to a "seasonal model".

He told councillors opening hours had been reduced and a fine dining experience they were offering had been scaled back.

Walsh said new strategy was being developed which would seek to break into the "untapped market" of people arriving in Inverness on tour buses.

The strategy predicts a 15% growth in ticket sales next year although it was acknowledged the attraction may not break even financially until 2029-30.

Highland Council is also due £1.156m in rent and officials have warned that the council may end up having to provide a total of £2.5m in additional support this year.

Council leader Raymond Bremner described the Inverness Castle Experience as a "massively new exciting project" but said he was concerned about the situation.

He said: "There is no getting away from it, the figures are disappointing.

"The numbers are not just below projection they were well below projection."

Cromarty Firth councillor John Edmonson said the figures were "pretty bad" and called for ticket prices to be examined.

"Invernessians and people in the Highlands, they always say we're charging too much," he said.

"Get more people in the door and then they spend more money in the various shops and whatever facilities are there."

Walsh said Highlife Highland had aimed for an affordable price, but added that it needed to consider market forces.

He said: "Certainly the pricing review is something that we will monitor carefully, use all the data we've got at our disposal and try to make good decisions going forward."

In a joint statement The Highland Council and Highlife Highland said visitor numbers and the associated income from retail and catering sales had been lower than originally projected.

They said: "This reflects a combination of factors, including a later-than-planned winter opening, which reduced the lead-in time normally required to develop key tourism markets and group bookings.

"Launching a new and distinctive visitor attraction is a long-term investment.

"Building awareness and establishing market presence takes time, particularly when introducing a unique experience to the tourism market."

They added that there was "strong interest" and a "growing profile" for the castle.

articles.title: Mid-air emergency declared on Londonderry-bound flight
articles.summary: A passenger thought she was "100% going to die" after a mid-air emergency was declared on her flight to Londonderry.
articles.body:
A passenger on a flight from London to Londonderry has said she thought she was going to die after a mid-air emergency was declared.

Joanne McLaughlin said they were told to prepare for the brace position while crossing the Irish Sea, and the "plane was definitely descending".

"When the first announcement was made, I 100% thought I was going to die, it was absolutely terrifying," McLaughlin said.

She was travelling on a Loganair flight from London Heathrow to the City of Derry airport on Thursday. It later emerged a cockpit windscreen had cracked. The Scottish airline said safety protocols had been followed.

McLaughlin, who lives in England and was visiting relatives in Derry, said after the initial announcement, they did not have another update for about 10 minutes.

"There were people on the plane who were visibility very distressed, I fully thought because we were over the sea when the emergency call was made, I thought the plane was going to crash into the sea," she said.

McLaughlin said the captain announced there was a crack in the windscreen in the cockpit and they had lowered the altitude to normalise cabin pressure.

They were then told the flight was planning to make an emergency landing at Belfast City airport, but shortly after the pilot confirmed it was safe enough to continue to Derry.

"I felt better when the captain said what the problem was because at least I knew it wasn't a catastrophic issue, but the initial announcement was so stark and left for so long before that update, it was too long," said McLaughlin.

The flight landed on time with all passengers and crew unharmed.

When they got to the gate, McLaughlin said the captain apologised for any anxiety the flight had caused.

McLaughlin said she felt that more after care should have been provided to passengers following the flight.

"There was 50 odd people on that plane who thought they were going to die, and when we landed, we were not offered anything or even to sit down for five minutes," she said.

McLaughlin said an email from the airline would have been appreciated.

A spokesperson for Loganair confirmed the flight "experienced an issue".

"As a precaution, the flight crew followed appropriate safety protocols, and the aircraft landed as normal," they added. "The safety and well-being of our passengers and crew remains our top priority."

A spokesperson for City of Derry Airport said a technical issue had been reported on an incoming Loganair flight from London.

"As a precaution, emergency services responded in line with established procedures," they said.

"We would like to thank all responding agencies for their prompt and professional response."

articles.summary: India News: MUMBAI: Atomic Energy Commission chairperson, A K Mohanty, and the US secretary of the department of energy Chris Wright, held discussions to explore .
articles.body: MUMBAI: Atomic Energy Commission chairperson, A K Mohanty, and the US secretary of the department of energy Chris Wright, held discussions to explore opportunities to further strengthen Indo-US nuclear ties for mutual benefit at the sidelines of an IAEA initiative for offshore atomic energy technologies in Washington on WednesdayInsiders in the nuclear fraternity in Mumbai said the talks gain significance in the context of India planning to attain 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047, which is expected to be achieved through government and private participation in the nuclear sector.The Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, passed by Parliament in Dec 2025, opened the doors for private participation in the Indian nuclear arena. articles.title: ‘Butcher of Bosnia’ Ratko Mladic — Convicted of Genocide for 1995 Massacre — Dead at 84
articles.summary: The "Butcher of Bosnia" died in a United Nations prison hospital Thursday, decades after he carried out a massacre of 8,000 Bosnian men and boys.
articles.body:
Ratko Mladic — known as the "butcher of Bosnia" for overseeing the 1995 massacre of 8,000 people — died Thursday while in United Nations custody. He was 84.

Mladic died in a prison hospital in The Hague, the U.N. said in a statement.

The reviled Mladic, who spent 14 years as a fugitive after the devastating wars in the nation then known as Yugoslavia, had suffered strokes and other health problems in recent years, according to reports, and was denied medical release in May.

Judge Graciela Gatti Santana , the head of the United Nations' International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, directed "a full inquiry into the circumstances" of Mladic's death, The Guardian reported .

In July 1995, Mladic commanded the Bosnian Serbian Army, which invaded the small town of Srebrenica, in eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, ultimately taking thousands of Bosnian Muslim boys and men to abuse, torture and execute. The community had been deemed a United Nations "safe area" when Mladic's army invaded.

The bodies were bulldozed into mass graves. At the time the mass killing was considered the worst atrocity in Europe since World War II.

Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra'ad al-Hussein once labeled Mladic the " epitome of evil" for his role in the Balkan war, which left more than 100,000 dead and more than 1 million homeless.

Mladic — who once directed his army to "scorch the brains" of Bosnian Muslims and at another point, declared himself a "Serbian God" — was taken into custody in 2011.

Mladic was convicted in 2017 of genocide and war crimes.

"Everything you said is pure lies. Shame on you!" he yelled after his conviction.

Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra'ad al-Hussein declared after Mladic's conviction that he was "the epitome of evil."

Mladic's son, Darko, was en route to The Hague after his father's death, according to PBS News.

articles.title: In 2021, Pennsylvania removed a failing 128-year-old dam; beneath the drained reservoir, Sterry Creek’s original channel was still intact after more than a century underwater
articles.summary: US News: The restoration project, led by conservation group The Nature Conservancy (TNC), focused on the aging O'Conner Reservoir dam inside the Dick and Nancy.
articles.body: The restoration project, led by conservation group The Nature Conservancy (TNC), focused on the aging O'Conner Reservoir dam inside the Dick and Nancy Eales Preserve at Moosic Mountain. Built in the late nineteenth century, the dam had held back water across a six-acre reservoir for generations. But years of wear and storm damage had made the structure increasingly unsafe. Field teams began carefully lowering the reservoir's water level before using pumps and specialist equipment to reduce pressure on the dam. In December 2021, crews excavated the main embankment. As the water drained away, researchers made an important discovery. The creek's original natural shape, gravel beds and winding path were still preserved beneath the old lakebed. Because the original waterway remained intact, managers no longer needed to build an expensive artificial stream channel. Instead, they allowed Sterry Creek to return to its historic route across the mountain ridge.Natural creek replaces artificial channelThe discovery changed the restoration plan. Stream restoration specialist Bill Weihbrecht worked with TNC stewardship directors on the project, making sure the reopened stream followed the natural shape of the valley. Pat McElhenny, director of stewardship for The Nature Conservancy's Pennsylvania chapter, led field operations to remove the middle section of the dam. Crews left parts of the original stone-lined spillway and outer dam walls in place to preserve some of the area's history while allowing water to flow naturally again. "The dam itself was at risk of failure and the pH level of the water was no longer conducive to aquatic species," documented the organisation in an official project review published by The Nature Conservancy. "TNC worked with local partners to perform a controlled demolition to lower the water level and allow the original stream to return to its original flow pattern. After the dam was breached and the reservoir drained, TNC's freshwater team was delighted to see that the original stream channel, which spent more than 100 years at the bottom of a reservoir, was still intact." Recent monitoring at the preserve has shown native plants returning across the drained lakebed. The area is also developing into a natural floodplain that can hold and slow seasonal floodwaters.Restored floodplain improves water healthBefore the dam was removed, the O'Conner Reservoir created slow-moving water with low oxygen levels, changed pH and higher temperatures. These conditions were harmful to native coldwater species. Draining the reservoir and reopening the old creek channel brought back faster natural water flow and cooler conditions needed by aquatic life. The former six-acre lakebed now works as a natural buffer during heavy rain. When storms cause Sterry Creek to rise, water can spread across the plant-covered floodplain instead of moving rapidly downstream towards populated areas. "The drained lakebed will now serve as a natural floodplain for Sterry Creek," TNC said in a project update covering Appalachian river reconnection projects. During periods of high water, wetland plants help slow the flow, trap sediment and absorb some of the excess runoff. Reconnecting the upper sections of Sterry Creek has also linked previously separated stream habitats to the wider Lackawanna River watershed. This gives native fish, amphibians and aquatic invertebrates greater access to connected waterways.Growing push to remove old damsThe return of Sterry Creek is part of a wider effort across the United States to remove old and unsafe dams. Environmental group American Rivers says hundreds of aging barriers have been removed from American waterways over the past decade to improve public safety and restore damaged rivers. Many old dams across the Appalachian region were built during the nineteenth century for mining, timber operations or early municipal water systems. After decades of limited or no use, many have become safety concerns, especially during extreme weather, while also blocking fish from moving through rivers. Pennsylvania state and federal agencies have increasingly supported removing old, unused dams instead of spending large amounts on repairs. The Sterry Creek project shows how removing an outdated structure can improve public safety while allowing a damaged ecosystem to begin recovering naturally. At the Dick and Nancy Eales Preserve at Moosic Mountain, the former reservoir is now becoming a recovering stream and wetland corridor. articles.summary: A Cuban illegal immigrant and a U.S. citizen allegedly stole luxury vehicles and artwork from a South Florida home after its owners died in a helicopter crash in Kenya.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A Cuban national whom ICE says is in the United States illegally is among two people accused of burglarizing a luxurious South Florida townhome whose owners were killed in a helicopter crash in Kenya. Geybert Alexander Garcia, 40, and Melany Pavon-Perdomo, 24, were arrested Aug. 25, according to arrest affidavits and Miami-Dade court records reviewed by Fox News Digital. Records show Garcia is a U.S. citizen. An ICE spokesperson told Fox News Digital that officers encountered Pavon-Perdomo at the Turner Guilford Knight Center after Coral Gables police arrested her on grand theft and burglary charges. ICE lodged a detainer with local authorities on Aug. 25, the spokesperson said. ICE said Pavon-Perdomo entered the United States at an unknown time and place, has not adjusted her immigration status and remains in the country illegally. The pair were accused of stealing two luxury vehicles, personal documents, jewelry and artwork — including a sculpture police valued at more than $500,000 — from the residence of Henry Parra, 55, and Adam Hlavaty, 42, who were among seven people killed Aug. 19 when a safari helicopter went down in northern Kenya. The property is appraised at nearly $3 million. The cause remains under investigation. The U.S. State Department said five of the people killed were U.S. citizens. The crash also killed Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte; José Suárez, who led Telemundo-owned stations in several Florida markets; Ecuador’s intelligence chief, Michele Sensi-Contugi; his wife, fashion designer Stephany Hollihan; and the pilot, Josh Outram. Hlavaty was a real estate executive and co-founder of a development company. "They were a loving couple who cherished their time together, especially traveling, making memories and enjoying life with their family and friends," friends said in a statement obtained by WSVN. "They were hardworking, generous and deeply committed to serving and giving back to their community." According to an arrest affidavit, the couple left their South Florida home Aug. 12 and had arranged for their housekeeper to visit daily. Investigators determined that the home and its contents were intact after the couple died, police said. articles.title: Shubman Gill dismisses Mohammed Siraj's injury concerns, says it 'takes time to come back to rhythm'

articles.body:
NEW DELHI: India captain Shubman Gill on Thursday ruled out any injury concern for Mohammed Siraj after the pacer appeared to be below his best during the drawn second Test against Sri Lanka in Colombo. Siraj bowled at a reduced pace and often used a shorter run-up during the Test. His fitness also came under the scanner after he landed heavily while trying to take a catch in Sri Lanka's first innings. Gill, however, made it clear that Siraj was not carrying an injury.

Gill said Siraj had not been feeling his best even during the first Test in Galle and was also returning to international cricket after a break. "Firstly, Siraj is not injured. He didn't feel well even in the first match (at Galle). He last played against Afghanistan in June…so he was playing almost after a couple of months. It takes time for someone to come back to the rhythm. "Even in the first Test, we felt that his pace was slow. But sometimes when you play more, you come back to the rhythm. But as far as the injury is concerned, there is nothing," he said. Siraj's lack of his usual pace was noticeable as India struggled to finish off Sri Lanka on the fifth day. The hosts batted through the final day, with Sonal Dinusha scoring an unbeaten 133 to secure a draw.

India had reduced Sri Lanka to 229/6 by the end of the fourth day but could not force the remaining wickets on the final day. "It gets very frustrating. We attacked a lot in the beginning. But I think as the match went on, the wicket got slower. It was not like the ball was not moving and when the ball was spinning, the wickets were not in play. It was not like the wicket was very flat," said Gill at the post-match press meet. The India captain said Sri Lanka's defensive approach made it difficult for his bowlers to create chances. "Unless you are playing a shot and looking to make a run, then it is difficult to take a wicket. We tried all that we could, and I don't think there was any lack of intensity or the efforts that we put in. The spinners bowled 50-60 overs on the trot for three days. "Fielding for three days is not an easy task in these conditions. I would say 10 out of 10 for the effort and the intent. They also played really well," he added. Gill also felt India could have been in a better position if they had taken their chances on the fourth day. "On day 4, we thought we had created chances. If there was a little more pressure, the wickets would have come and then maybe the result would have been better. But as long as we still have a chance to qualify for the World Test Championship (final), it's fine."

Gill was pleased with the progress made by Prasidh Krishna. "I think he's been in the pick of our bowlers. When things are not happening, he's been our go-to bowler, especially this season. He's created chances, which is what I want as a captain. We want a go-to bowler when wickets are not guaranteed. I think he did that brilliantly," he said.
